title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
authors: Jarno Platenburg, Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Paola Cinnella, Patrick Gallinari
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

infographic.key_insight: TurtLES benchmarks neural PDE surrogates on realistic 3D turbulent wakes, exposing instability and loss of small-scale energy during autoregressive rollouts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark tests whether learned CFD surrogates can handle long-horizon turbulent flows on irregular meshes at industrially relevant resolution.
method: Generate 3D cylinder wakes using high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations.
Vary geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack.
Evaluate neural operators through autoregressive temporal rollouts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 14 TB dataset contains 400 trajectories with 400 time steps each and 3–11 million points per frame.
infographic.watch_item: Large irregular meshes pose substantial data-handling and learning challenges, while rollout stability remains a key concern.
infographic.paper_title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates

title: Projection-based segregated, iterative, and multi-stage physics-informed neural network for incompressible Navier-stokes equations
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Zhixiang Ling, Yinghao Huo, Huayong Liu, Yunde Su
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks(PINNs) offer a mesh-free and continuously differentiable approach to fluid simulation. However, standard monolithic PINNs for incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations often suffer from severe constraint coupling and spectral biases, limiting both convergence and accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a segregated, iterative, and multi-stage PINN (SIM-PINN) inspired by the classical projection method in computational fluid dynamics. In SIM-PINN, the nonlinear NS equations are decoupled into the linearized momentum and pressure Poisson equations. Each is addressed separately using dedicated multi-stage neural networks and coupled through projection-based inner iterations. Each stage of the multi-stage neural networks for the momentum equations corresponds to one iteration of the projection method, in which the velocity fields are progressively refined at targeted frequencies. Upon iteration convergence, solutions to the fully coupled and nonlinear NS equations are recovered. By integrating the segregated and iterative framework with the multi-stage training, SIM-PINN alleviates the optimization difficulties of the incompressible NS equations arising from nonlinearity, constraint coupling, and spectral biases. The improved convergence and accuracy are demonstrated by simulations of steady lid-driven cavity and unsteady Kolmogorov flows.

infographic.key_insight: SIM-PINN combines projection-based decoupling, iterative coupling, and multi-stage neural networks to improve convergence and accuracy for incompressible Navier–Stokes equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a mesh-free route to incompressible flow simulation while addressing optimization difficulties caused by nonlinear dynamics, coupled constraints, and spectral bias.
method: Separate the Navier–Stokes system into linearized momentum and pressure Poisson equations.
Solve the subproblems with dedicated multi-stage neural networks linked by projection-based inner iterations.
Progressively refine velocity fields at targeted frequencies, recovering the coupled nonlinear solution upon convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved convergence and accuracy on steady lid-driven cavity and unsteady Kolmogorov flow simulations, without quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Computational cost and scalability beyond the two demonstrated flow cases are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Projection-based segregated, iterative, and multi-stage physics-informed neural network for incompressible Navier-stokes equations

title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence
authors: Marco Edoardo Rosti, Andrea Mazzino
abstract: Most turbulent flows are sustained by inertia, which transfers energy across scales and produces characteristic power-law spectra. Yet dilute polymer solutions also exhibit turbulence when inertia is negligible: in this state, known as elastic turbulence, the velocity field remains spatially smooth while both the velocity and the polymer conformation exhibit robust power-law spectra. How a smooth flow, lacking a hierarchy of eddies, generates such multiscale structure has remained unexplained. Here we show that the missing mechanism is elastic frontogenesis, whereby the flow spontaneously organizes polymer stress into thin sheets that are stretched within their plane and compressed across their thickness, causing their amplitude to grow as they become thinner. Because the fronts are sheet-like structures, this amplification-thinning law uniquely determines the polymer conformation spectrum, while the Stokes response transfers the same geometric scaling to the velocity field, reconciling broadband spectra with spatial smoothness. Being geometric rather than model-specific, elastic frontogenesis provides an organizing principle for viscoelastic flows and the viscoelastic analogue of vortex stretching in inertial turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Elastic frontogenesis creates thin, intensifying polymer-stress sheets whose geometry explains power-law spectra despite a spatially smooth velocity field.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mechanism offers a framework for interpreting multiscale fluctuations in polymer-solution flows where inertia is negligible.
method: Identify sheet-like polymer-stress fronts stretched in-plane and compressed across their thickness.
Relate front amplification and thinning to the polymer conformation spectrum.
Use the Stokes response to connect this geometric scaling to the velocity spectrum.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports robust power-law spectra in velocity and polymer conformation but provides no numerical exponents, evaluation details, or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish how broadly the proposed geometric scaling holds across constitutive models and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence

title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
authors: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song
abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.

infographic.key_insight: A parameterized physics-informed neural network predicts 3D microfluidic cooling performance across a continuous geometric design space, with reported computational savings exceeding four orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate could accelerate the design and optimization of embedded manifold microchannels for cooling high-performance electronic chips.
method: Inputs combine four geometric dimensions with three spatial coordinates.
Training combines geometric ansatz embedding, SOAP optimization, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum.
An optimized JAX backend enables convergence in under four hours on one consumer-grade GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against finite-element simulations, the abstract reports relative errors of 8.1% for velocity fields and 5.6% for temperature fields.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish accuracy outside the trained geometric design space or validation against physical experiments.
infographic.paper_title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling

title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
authors: Beatriz Fagá, Georgii Oblapenko, Yiyang Zhu, Daniel Doehring, Manuel Torrilhon
abstract: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.

infographic.key_insight: High-order discontinuous Galerkin spectral element simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet agree with reference finite-volume solvers for complex hypersonic flow with shock–shock interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DGSEM offers an alternative to conventional second-order finite-volume methods for modeling high-enthalpy propulsion flows where numerical dissipation can demand refined meshes.
method: Use high-order DGSEM with element-local polynomial bases.
Simulate a two-dimensional scramjet configuration.
Compare results against reference finite-volume solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with reference finite-volume results, supporting implementation verification, but gives no quantitative error or runtime metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The reported two-dimensional comparison does not establish computational savings or accuracy for three-dimensional turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows

title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
authors: Fehmi Najar
abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

infographic.key_insight: Retaining one fluid relaxation mode is essential to predict nonlinear microbeam response and dynamic pull-in; adding coupled modes cannot replace it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A compact fluid–structure model supports assessment of stable operating ranges and pull-in risk in electrostatic MEMS with squeeze-film damping.
method: Build a reduced-order model from complex modes of the coupled fluid–structure system.
Continue periodic responses in the frequency domain and assess stability using Floquet multipliers.
Map attraction basins, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in using three real unknowns.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was validated against measured and computed microswitch frequency responses, and one fluid mode was necessary and sufficient for all simulated devices.
infographic.watch_item: Single-fluid-mode sufficiency is demonstrated for the simulated devices, not universally; strongly coupled films require a correction.
infographic.paper_title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping

title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
authors: Wolfgang Flachberger, Lukas Einkemmer
abstract: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.

infographic.key_insight: Minimum dissipation in driven stationary systems and maximum dissipation during frozen-state relaxation arise from the same convex, minimized Rayleighian framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework clarifies how variational formulations can recover dissipative flow equations while accounting for energy transport and inertia.
method: Analyze thermodynamic extremal properties across stationary and relaxation regimes.
Use Reynolds transport to formulate continuum energy rates and hold inertial driving forces fixed during variation.
Switch to material coordinates for Navier–Stokes flow to remove the explicit convective acceleration term.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical tests on Stokes, unsteady Stokes, Navier–Stokes flow, and dissipative Lagrangian mechanics, but no numerical benchmarks or experimental data.
infographic.watch_item: With inertia, an extremal statement requires the frozen driving force to be independent of the varied rate, demanding careful choices of variables and coordinates.
infographic.paper_title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality

title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Guglielmo Padula, Antonio Colanera, Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: We present SPOD-GPR, a non-intrusive, parametric, spatio-temporal reduced-order model (ROM) that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Spectral POD (SPOD), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). A parametric POD first projects the high-dimensional state onto a low-dimensional subspace. The reduced trajectories are then divided into windowed sections, transformed into the frequency domain, and truncated to the most energetic frequencies. SPOD is then performed independently at each retained frequency, yielding temporally coherent modes and coefficients. The parametric dependence of the POD and SPOD bases is modelled by GPR on a local chart of the Grassmann manifold after Procrustes alignment. The SPOD modal coefficients are learned both as explicit functions of the parameters and through a parameter-conditioned autoregressive model that allows for temporal extrapolation beyond the training window. Gaussian processes are sampled jointly and pathwise via Matheron conditioning, ensuring that each predictive realization carries uncertainty quantification consistent with the posterior distribution. The method is tested on four parametric examples where the parameter values and the prediction horizon lie outside the training data: the two-dimensional anisotropic Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation in a time-periodic and a travelling-wave regime, each parametrised by one of its two coefficients; flow past a cylinder parametrised by the Reynolds number; and flow past an elliptic obstacle parametrised by its semi-axes. In all cases, SPOD-GPR reduces the normalised mean absolute error compared to a POD-GPR baseline, and improves the calibration of the predictive uncertainty, especially in the fluid flow cases, where POD-GPR is severely overconfident. This opens the way to spectral, uncertainty-aware reduced-order models for many-query and real-time applications, such as digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: SPOD-GPR combines spectral structure and Gaussian process regression to improve parametric flow predictions and uncertainty calibration over a POD-GPR baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports uncertainty-aware surrogate modelling for many-query and real-time applications, including fluid-flow digital twins.
method: Compress states with parametric POD, then window trajectories and retain energetic frequencies.
Apply SPOD at each retained frequency and learn parameter-dependent bases using aligned Grassmann charts and GPR.
Learn spectral coefficients directly and autoregressively; sample predictions jointly using Matheron conditioning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four parametric tests—two Kuramoto–Sivashinsky regimes, cylinder flow, and elliptic-obstacle flow—with parameters and prediction horizons outside training data, SPOD-GPR reduced normalised mean absolute error and improved uncertainty calibration versus POD-GPR.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and uncertainty calibration beyond the tested parameter ranges and prediction horizons remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression

title: Phase-resolved turbulence dynamics in cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow
authors: Xinyu Wang, Yan Bao, Benlong Wang
abstract: Direct numerical simulations examine the phase-dependent turbulence dynamics of pipe flow driven by cardiac-cycle-inspired waveforms. Four cases with and without a low-flow plateau span two Reynolds-number ranges. The response follows four stages of turbulent--turbulent reorganisation. Strong acceleration suppresses transverse fluctuations and vortical activity. During acceleration and early deceleration, streamwise-normal-stress production recovers ahead of pressure--strain redistribution and radial momentum transport, allowing energy to accumulate in elongated streaks. In early deceleration, near-wall high-speed streaks develop predominantly varicose disturbances associated with Q4 sweeps, whereas outer-buffer-layer low-speed streaks develop predominantly sinuous disturbances associated with Q2 ejections. The transition exhibits distinct radial sequences: Q2-based local onset occurs progressively later towards the wall, whereas Q4-based onset is nearly simultaneous across the viscous sublayer and buffer layer, with peaks occurring successively outwards. The two responses overlap between the drag minimum and recovery maximum as redistribution intensifies markedly and multiscale momentum transport recovers rapidly. Turbulence then decays and its scales readjust. Where present, the plateau prolongs this decay and weakens the turbulence inherited by the next acceleration stage. It further delays local instability and lengthens the onset-to-peak intervals of the shear contributions. An unsteady friction decomposition links these phase-dependent dynamics to the drag response, highlighting the role of delayed turbulent shear recovery in sustaining the low-drag interval.

infographic.key_insight: Cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsation suppresses turbulence during acceleration, while delayed turbulent shear recovery sustains a low-drag interval before turbulence reorganises.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Phase-resolved links between pulsation, turbulence recovery and drag can inform waveform design for pulsatile pipe-flow systems.
method: Direct numerical simulations of four waveform-driven pipe-flow cases across two Reynolds-number ranges.
Comparison of waveforms with and without a low-flow plateau.
Phase-resolved turbulence analysis and unsteady friction decomposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the simulated cases, streamwise-stress production recovers before redistribution and radial transport, while a low-flow plateau prolongs decay and delays local instability.
infographic.watch_item: The findings cover four simulated pipe-flow cases; applicability to broader Reynolds numbers, complex geometries or physiological flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Phase-resolved turbulence dynamics in cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow

title: Bathyspheres, dust devils, lunar plumes and Martian drones: a generalised mathematical model for particle-fluid flow fields generated by static particle bed entrainment across macroscopic scales
authors: S. Langdon, D. J. Needham
abstract: We consider a recently derived mathematical model for the mechanism by which a wind driven flow entrains particles into a fluid from an otherwise static particle bed, a process that is fundamental in initiating and driving the phenomenon of particle cloud formation. This model was previously applied to the "helicopter brownout" problem, in which, as a helicopter descends towards a bed of sand, the downwash and swirling flow from the rotors entrain particles into the air, forming a high-velocity particle-laden cloud around the helicopter. Here, we define a new measure of particle cloud formation potential, outline how the model can be incorporated into existing Computational Fluid Dynamics software, and extend the model to scenarios including: formation of particle clouds in the absence of swirl, such as those caused by a bathysphere descending to the ocean bed, or a rocket landing on the lunar surface, in which case we can precisely predict the critical height above the surface at which particle cloud formation is initiated; generation of dust clouds by less powerful downwash and swirling flows caused by drones or other smaller rotorcraft, such as NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter, in which case gravitational effects are included in the model; formation of dust devils (dust clouds formed within and around an upwardly circulating columnar air flow), in which case downwash is replaced by updraft. In each case, predictive models are derived through minor adaptations to key modelling assumptions.

infographic.key_insight: A generalised mathematical model predicts particle-bed entrainment and cloud formation across rotorcraft, bathysphere, lunar-landing and dust-devil flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support CFD predictions of sediment or dust clouds that affect visibility and operations near particle-covered surfaces.
method: Define a measure of particle-cloud formation potential.
Adapt entrainment assumptions for swirl-free flows, gravity-sensitive rotorcraft flows and updrafts.
Outline integration into existing CFD software.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports predictive model derivations, including a critical cloud-initiation height for swirl-free cases, but provides no experimental validation or quantitative accuracy results.
infographic.watch_item: Predictive accuracy across environments remains to be validated, particularly where adapting the modelling assumptions changes the dominant physics.
infographic.paper_title: Bathyspheres, dust devils, lunar plumes and Martian drones: a generalised mathematical model for particle-fluid flow fields generated by static particle bed entrainment across macroscopic scales

title: Flash evaporation Riemann Problem: Thermodynamic Relaxation and Oscillation-Free Real Fluid Finite Volume Method
authors: Haotong Bai, Ping Yi, Yixin Yang, Guoyan Zhao, Wenjia Xie, Mingbo Sun
abstract: The Flash evaporation Riemann problem (FeRP) formulated the wave structures of flash evaporation in the vapor-liquid homogeneous equilibrium limit. However, physical flash evaporation involves finite-rate interphase heat and mass transfer, inducing the wave structure to deviate from the equilibrium state. To solve such a non-equilibrium Riemann problem, this paper first derives the governing equation of mechanical equilibrium evolution in a relaxation system, based on which an oscillation-free Homogeneous Relaxation Real Fluid (HRRF) finite volume method is developed. In addition to the Euler equations with mass relaxation, the HRRF method evolves advection equations for the internal energy--pressure affine parameters and the vapor volume fraction, in order to eliminate numerical pressure oscillations inherent in conservative methods while preserving phase-transition-induced pressure changes, and consistently degenerate into a completely pressure-equilibrium method in supercritical flows. The HRRF method is then employed to comprehensively evaluate how thermodynamic relaxation affects the FeRP solution. Results indicate that the non-classical expansion shock of the FeRP loses its traveling-wave characteristics with increasing relaxation time, continuously degenerating into a self-similar rarefaction wave. Compared with the equilibrium limit, an increased mass transfer relaxation time smooths the expansion branch of the RP solution, lowers the intermediate pressure and velocity, and induces a pseudo-splitting of the rarefaction wave as well as a pseudo-advance of the phase transition onset. Meanwhile, the heat transfer relaxation time primarily dictates the temperature difference in the vapor-liquid mixture, thereby modulating the liquid superheat and in turn influencing the mass transfer rate.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-rate thermodynamic relaxation transforms the flash-evaporation expansion shock toward a self-similar rarefaction wave as relaxation time increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports more reliable simulation of rapid flashing flows by suppressing spurious pressure oscillations while retaining physical phase-change pressure dynamics.
method: Derive mechanical-equilibrium evolution equations for a thermodynamic relaxation system.
Develop a Homogeneous Relaxation Real Fluid finite-volume method coupling Euler equations with mass relaxation.
Advect internal energy–pressure affine parameters and vapor volume fraction to maintain pressure consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: Flash-evaporation Riemann-problem evaluations show that longer mass-transfer relaxation times smooth expansion and lower intermediate pressure and velocity, while heat-transfer relaxation controls phase temperature differences.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports Riemann-problem evaluations but does not establish experimental validation or robustness for multidimensional engineering flows.
infographic.paper_title: Flash evaporation Riemann Problem: Thermodynamic Relaxation and Oscillation-Free Real Fluid Finite Volume Method

title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
authors: Matthew N. Crowe
abstract: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.

infographic.key_insight: A semi-analytical method constructs propagating dipolar vortices, or modons, in vertically sheared flows with arbitrarily many quasi-geostrophic fluid layers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports idealized modeling of coherent ocean vortices that can transport fluid over long distances.
method: Represent stratified flow using an N-layer quasi-geostrophic framework.
Construct modon solutions semi-analytically in a vertically sheared background flow.
Examine interlayer differences and depth-dependent potential-vorticity gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three example modons illustrating effects of interlayer variation and potential-vorticity gradients associated with surface deformation and velocity shear.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report observational validation or stability testing of the constructed solutions.
infographic.paper_title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow

title: Sub-filter-scale stress and heat flux in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer
authors: Raagvendra Singh, Sabbir Ahmed, Lian Duan, Carlo Scalo, Takahiko Toki
abstract: A comparative study of sub-filter-scale (SFS) quantities in hypersonic Couette flow and flat-plate boundary layer turbulence under strongly cooled-wall conditions is carried out using filtered direct numerical simulation (DNS) data to characterize the differences in SFS dynamics between internal and external wall-bounded turbulence. The two flows exhibit similar near-wall behaviour in the mean velocity profiles and SFS stress components; however, marked differences emerge in the outer layer and thermal structure. The two configurations also exhibit different thermal fields, leading to different temperature-velocity relations. The SFS behaviour shows strong sensitivity to the filtering operation: the top-hat filter yields larger SFS magnitudes, whereas the sharp spectral filter preserves a distinct spectral separation near the cutoff, leading to characteristic SFS features. Decomposition of the SFS terms shows that the residual component provides the dominant contribution to the mean SFS shear stress and heat flux. Differences between the two flows are primarily associated with the interaction terms between the resolved and residual components, which contribute with opposite signs in the two configurations, consistent with their different thermal structures. The different thermal structures also lead to distinct SFS heat-flux behaviour, including a sign change in the flat-plate boundary layer. Instantaneous SFS fields further reveal that local extrema arise from the combined contributions of multiple decomposed terms. Although these terms exhibit large local fluctuations, their net contributions to the averaged SFS quantities are relatively small. The trace of the SFS stress exhibits local negative values, reflecting local energy redistribution across the filter scale rather than a loss of physical energy.

infographic.key_insight: Hypersonic Couette flow and flat-plate boundary layers share near-wall SFS stress behaviour but differ in outer-layer and thermal dynamics, including a heat-flux sign change in the boundary layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SFS closures for hypersonic simulations should account for flow-dependent thermal structure and filter choice rather than assume universal stress and heat-flux behaviour.
method: Compare filtered DNS of both flows under strongly cooled-wall conditions.
Evaluate top-hat and sharp spectral filters.
Decompose SFS stresses and heat fluxes into resolved, residual and interaction contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Filtered DNS shows that residual contributions dominate mean SFS shear stress and heat flux, while resolved–residual interactions contribute with opposite signs in the two flows.
infographic.watch_item: The findings concern strongly cooled walls and are filter-sensitive; generalization to other thermal conditions requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Sub-filter-scale stress and heat flux in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer

title: Velocity gradient tensor reconstruction from tracer orientations via Jeffery dynamics
authors: Isshin Arai, Tomoaki Itano
abstract: The velocity gradient tensor is a local quantity, but methods that obtain it by spatial differencing of the velocities of spherical tracers amplify measurement noise. We propose a method that reconstructs the velocity gradient tensor from the orientations of non-spherical tracers such as flakes and rods. Based on the Jeffery-type equation, we show that, for incompressible flow, all components of the velocity gradient tensor are uniquely determined from the orientations of four tracers and their time derivatives in the neighbourhood of a reference point (orientation-based method). The method uses neither tracer positions nor spatial differencing. It therefore requires orientation measurements only near the reference point, without requiring measurements throughout a three-dimensional region, and measurement noise is amplified only through temporal differencing. Consequently, the minimum achievable error scales as $σ^{1/2}$ with the noise level $σ$, compared with $σ^{1/3}$ for the positional PTV-plus-differencing approach (position-based method). Numerical tests further show that the vorticity is reconstructed more accurately than by the position-based method, whereas the strain rate is reconstructed with comparable accuracy. Finally, applying the method to spherical Couette flow, we find that the reconstruction fails where the neighbouring tracers align, which renders the inversion ill-conditioned, and that this degeneracy appears as the characteristic light-and-dark pattern familiar from flow visualization.

infographic.key_insight: For incompressible flow, four non-spherical tracers’ orientations and time derivatives can uniquely determine the local velocity gradient tensor when the inversion is nondegenerate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Orientation-based reconstruction could reduce measurement-noise sensitivity and spatial sampling requirements for local flow-gradient diagnostics.
method: Measure nearby rod or flake orientations and their time derivatives.
Invert Jeffery-type dynamics to recover the velocity gradient tensor.
Avoid tracer positions and spatial differencing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show more accurate vorticity and comparable strain-rate reconstruction versus position-based estimation; the analysis predicts minimum error scaling as σ^(1/2), versus σ^(1/3).
infographic.watch_item: Aligned tracers make the inversion ill-conditioned, causing reconstruction failure in parts of spherical Couette flow.
infographic.paper_title: Velocity gradient tensor reconstruction from tracer orientations via Jeffery dynamics

title: Thermochemical Rossby waves in rapid rotation: from swallowtail geometry to nonlinear selection
authors: Oleg N. Kirillov
abstract: When heat and solute both destabilise a rapidly rotating fluid, do their buoyancies add? Codensity models assume so, giving a straight onset diagonal; spherical shells show curved and kinked thresholds. We study the Busse--Simitev rotating annulus, whose normal modes obey an exact complex cubic dispersion relation. Combining the Bilharz criterion with the neutral-curve envelope yields, in the rapid-rotation limit, an explicit swallowtail wave front, in Arnold's sense, that bends the codensity diagonal into smooth and then kinked thresholds as the diffusivity ratio decreases. Its cusp edges lie inside the unstable domain and its exposed kink ends at the swallowtail singularity; these are singularities of wave-number selection, without coalescence of temporal eigenvalues, and the swallowtail diffusivity ratio has analytical small- and large-Prandtl-number limits. At a kink, broad, fast thermal and narrow, slow compositional Rossby waves become neutral together; hidden arcs mark the birth and merger of unstable wave-number bands. The same geometry enters nonlinear selection: mean-scalar feedback factors through neutral-arc normals and scalar responses, so the mean-profile coexistence margin vanishes with the kink angle as the waves merge. Complete cubic coefficients predict robust coexistence at a reference corner and a narrow bistable interval near merger. Exact finite-rotation corners and periodic-cell simulations confirm the coexisting waves and their invasion thresholds.

infographic.key_insight: Thermal and compositional buoyancy interact through a swallowtail onset geometry, producing kinked instability thresholds and selecting distinct Rossby waves rather than simply adding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results caution against additive-buoyancy approximations when predicting instability and competing flow patterns in rapidly rotating, double-diffusive fluids.
method: Analyze the rotating-annulus model’s exact cubic dispersion relation using the Bilharz stability criterion.
Derive rapid-rotation neutral-curve envelopes and their swallowtail geometry.
Evaluate nonlinear wave selection through mean-scalar feedback and cubic amplitude coefficients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Exact finite-rotation corner calculations and periodic-cell simulations confirm coexisting thermal and compositional waves and their invasion thresholds.
infographic.watch_item: The onset geometry is derived in a rapid-rotation annulus model; quantitative transfer to spherical shells or engineering systems requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Thermochemical Rossby waves in rapid rotation: from swallowtail geometry to nonlinear selection

title: Hydrograd v2.0: a differentiable two-dimensional shallow-water model on unstructured meshes with steady and unsteady adjoints for calibration and closure learning
authors: Xiaofeng Liu
abstract: We present \textit{Hydrograd} v2.0, a significantly improved differentiable 2D shallow-water model written in Python with JAX. The model solves the shallow-water equations on the unstructured meshes of production models such as SRH-2D and HEC-RAS 2D with a well-balanced, positivity-preserving finite-volume scheme that handles wetting and drying. Gradients are tailored to the type of problem. Steady states are found by Newton's method with an exact sparse Jacobian obtained by graph colouring, and their gradients follow from the implicit function theorem at the cost of one linear solve. Unsteady flows are differentiated in reverse mode with checkpointing, or with an implicit time integrator whose gradient costs about two forward runs. All gradients agree with finite differences, to about $10^{-8}$ for steady flows. On the Savannah River case, the steady water surface differs from that of SRH-2D by 4.7\,mm (root mean square). Steady closure learning was 96 times faster than differentiating through time marching and reached a lower loss. An inflow hydrograph was inverted from stage records with a peak error of 2\,\%. In an unsteady roughness calibration, a singular value decomposition analysis of the sensitivity matrix showed that the stage records at the gauges are 70 to 160 times more sensitive to the total resistance of the reach than to its distribution among the roughness zones, which explains why only a gauge layout with gauges in every zone recovered all five roughness values. On one GPU, a mesh of 512,000 cells takes 7.6\,s for a forward run and 51\,s for a gradient.

infographic.key_insight: Hydrograd v2.0 makes unstructured-mesh shallow-water simulations differentiable, enabling efficient parameter calibration and closure learning with steady and unsteady adjoints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports hydraulic calibration on meshes from production models such as SRH-2D and HEC-RAS 2D, including flows with wetting and drying.
method: Python/JAX finite-volume solver with well-balanced, positivity-preserving treatment.
Newton steady solves with graph-coloured sparse Jacobians; implicit gradients require one linear solve.
Unsteady gradients via checkpointed reverse mode or an implicit time integrator.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported tests show steady gradients agreeing with finite differences to about 10⁻⁸, Savannah River water-surface RMSE of 4.7 mm versus SRH-2D, and steady closure learning 96× faster than differentiation through time marching.
infographic.watch_item: Spatial roughness calibration is sensitive to gauge placement: recovering all five zone values required gauges in every zone in the reported test.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrograd v2.0: a differentiable two-dimensional shallow-water model on unstructured meshes with steady and unsteady adjoints for calibration and closure learning

title: Quantitative global regularity for Navier--Stokes equations with odd viscosity on the cubic three-torus
authors: Jinzheng Li, Yuqi Li, Hao-Yu Sun
abstract: We study the three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equation on the cubic torus with a constant odd-viscosity operator given by the vertical derivative of the curl. Arbitrary real, mean-zero, divergence-free initial data and an independent steady force, both in the second-order Sobolev space, admit a unique global strong solution when the magnitude of one fixed odd-viscosity coefficient is at least a norm-uniform sufficient threshold. In the unforced case the solution is smooth at positive times. The qualitative argument adapts the resonant-averaging framework for rapidly rotating fluids to the different odd-viscous dispersion. Weighted lattice counts and signed corrected-energy estimates yield a sufficient bound for the odd-to-ordinary viscosity ratio that is polynomial in the normalized initial-data radius at each fixed normalized force radius, together with a separate bound in a specified force-dominated regime. No optimality is claimed for the polynomial exponents or prefactors; determining the sharp viscosity threshold for the original equation remains open. Direct kinetic and weighted enstrophy barriers also give regularity for every coefficient on explicit bounded data and force regions, including the closed unforced ball of homogeneous second-order Fourier Sobolev radius ninety-seven fortieths times the viscosity and seven closed forced rectangles. We specify how finite certificates enter the analytic argument and distinguish minimization of a sufficient formula from sharpness for the original equation. All three main theorems are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

infographic.key_insight: Sufficiently strong odd viscosity guarantees unique global strong solutions for 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes flow on the cubic torus, with explicit bounds tied to initial-data and forcing norms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These rigorous stability bounds may inform numerical studies of odd-viscous flows, but the paper does not develop a CFD surrogate or validate an engineering application.
method: Adapt resonant averaging to the dispersion induced by the vertical derivative of curl.
Combine weighted lattice counts and corrected-energy estimates to derive sufficient viscosity thresholds.
Use kinetic and weighted-enstrophy barriers for bounded-data regimes; formally verify all three main theorems in Lean 4.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evidence is mathematical rather than empirical: the abstract reports polynomial sufficient thresholds, an explicit unforced regularity ball, seven closed forced rectangles, and Lean 4 verification.
infographic.watch_item: The thresholds are sufficient, not proven sharp, and apply to a specific constant odd-viscosity operator on a periodic cubic domain.
infographic.paper_title: Quantitative global regularity for Navier--Stokes equations with odd viscosity on the cubic three-torus

title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure
authors: Frimpong A. Baidoo, Narayana R. Aluru, Thomas J. R. Hughes, Michael R. A. Abdelmalik
abstract: We assess the non-linear version of the Entropy Stable Extension to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations which were originally derived in arXiv:2407.17334. Using an identity for the derivative of the inverse of linearized collision operator, we show that the Entropy Stable Extension takes the form of a fourth-order quasi-cubic system of equations when written in entropy variables. Furthermore, we find that the quasi-linear contributions to the extension retain the highest order derivative contributions and the entropy stability of the full extension. This quasi-linear approximation is applied to the stationary heat transfer between parallel plates where we find that a specification of the boundary conditions that interpolates between the continuum and collisions limits can yield temperature profiles that better agree with DSMC predictions than Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with Smoluchowski boundary conditions, while also giving a heat flux prediction that better agrees with the Sherman-Lees heat flux than the Navier-Stokes-Fourier prediction. We conclude with a brief study of dispersion of plane waves according to the linearized equations in one dimension where we show that all frequency modes are stable and relate this to entropy stability.

infographic.key_insight: The nonlinear entropy-stable extension of Navier–Stokes–Fourier becomes a fourth-order quasi-cubic system in entropy variables, while its quasi-linear approximation preserves the highest-order derivatives and entropy stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The closure offers a continuum-model route to improved rarefied-gas heat-transfer predictions between parallel plates.
method: Reformulate the nonlinear closure using entropy variables and an inverse-collision-operator derivative identity.
Apply an entropy-stable quasi-linear approximation to stationary parallel-plate heat transfer.
Analyze plane-wave dispersion in the one-dimensional linearized equations.
infographic.evidence_signal: With boundary conditions interpolating between continuum and collisionless limits, temperature profiles agree better with DSMC and heat flux agrees better with Sherman–Lees than Navier–Stokes–Fourier predictions; all modes in the linearized dispersion study are stable.
infographic.watch_item: Reported heat-transfer gains depend on the boundary-condition specification, and the abstract does not establish performance for multidimensional or turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure

title: Tuning fluid frictional drag through flow-induced aggregation of wormlike micelles
authors: Lucas Warwaruk, Amanda Tiano, Berith Isaac, Gareth H. McKinley
abstract: Charged amphiphilic surfactants are versatile polymorphic molecules which can form supramolecular structures, such as wormlike micelles. We study the rheology and non-Newtonian fluid dynamics of the cationic surfactant trimethyltetradecylammonium chloride (TTAC) combined with the aromatic counter-ion sodium salicylate (NaSal). In the non-dilute regime, this solution exhibits a linear viscoelastic response consistent with a single-mode Jeffreys model, and in capillary pinch-off experiments, fluid filaments form extended cylindrical threads, indicating strong strain-stiffening. In the dilute regime the linear viscoelasticity and extensional rheology become immeasurably small, but the TTAC/NaSal mixture develops flow-induced structures at high shear rates, as the result of an end-to-end concatenation of micelles produced by shear-induced flow alignment. These flow-induced structures augment both the measured viscosity and the viscous drag in laminar flows at high shear rates (by as much as 50 %). In turbulent Taylor-Couette flow, the flow-induced structures produce a sudden and dramatic destabilizing influence on the stable toroidal Taylor vortices, resulting in upwards of a 200 % enhancement in turbulent drag. However, with increasing Reynolds number, the turbulent flow transitions smoothly to a state of drag reduction, generating up to a 30 % reduction in fluid frictional drag but without the shear-induced degradation that plagues drag reduction strategies based on solutions of high molecular weight polymer, such as polyacrylamide. These results show that surfactants are a unique and effective modifier of fluid frictional drag in both laminar and turbulent flow regimes, capable of producing both significant levels of drag enhancement and drag reduction by tuning the composition and operating conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Flow-induced aggregation of TTAC/NaSal wormlike micelles can switch fluid friction from strong drag enhancement to drag reduction as flow conditions change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Surfactant additives offer tunable friction control without the shear-induced degradation associated with high-molecular-weight polymer drag reducers.
method: Characterize TTAC/NaSal solutions using linear rheology and capillary pinch-off experiments.
Measure high-shear viscosity and laminar drag as flow-induced micellar structures develop.
Evaluate turbulent drag and vortex stability in Taylor–Couette flow across Reynolds numbers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports up to 50% laminar drag enhancement, upwards of 200% turbulent drag enhancement, and up to 30% turbulent drag reduction at higher Reynolds numbers.
infographic.watch_item: Composition and operating conditions require careful selection because flow-induced aggregation can substantially increase drag before the drag-reducing regime is reached.
infographic.paper_title: Tuning fluid frictional drag through flow-induced aggregation of wormlike micelles

title: Turbulent wakes behind nine bluff-body shapes from direct numerical simulation and particle image velocimetry
authors: Zhen Zhang, Theo Käufer, Louise Ronglan, Michael S. Triantafyllou, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: We present a cross-validated dataset of turbulent wakes behind nine bluff bodies at Reynolds number Re = 10,000: a circular cylinder, a 2:1 elliptical cylinder at 0° and 90°, short and long isosceles triangles with the apex upstream or downstream, and a square cylinder at 0° and 45°. Each body was studied by wall-resolved direct numerical simulation (DNS) with a spectral-element solver and by time-resolved planar particle image velocimetry (PIV) in the MIT Intelligent Towing Tank. The DNS records contain time- and spanwise-averaged velocity, pressure and Reynolds stresses, 24-bin phase-averaged fields keyed to the lift signal, drag and lift histories, and one three-dimensional instantaneous snapshot per body; the PIV records contain the matching time-mean and phase-averaged fields in the same coordinate frame. The DNS set-up is verified against reference cylinder data at Re = 3900, and DNS and PIV at Re = 10,000 are compared field by field. The dataset supports the development and testing of data-driven turbulence closures, reduced-order models, and wake-stability analyses across geometries with distinct separation behavior.

infographic.key_insight: A cross-validated DNS–PIV dataset captures turbulent wakes behind nine bluff-body geometries at Re = 10,000, enabling comparisons across distinct separation behaviors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The dataset supports development and testing of data-driven turbulence closures, reduced-order models, and wake-stability analyses across geometries.
method: Wall-resolved spectral-element DNS for nine bluff-body shapes and orientations.
Time-resolved planar PIV in the MIT Intelligent Towing Tank.
Matched mean fields and 24-bin phase averages keyed to the lift signal.
infographic.evidence_signal: The DNS setup is verified against reference cylinder data at Re = 3900, and DNS and PIV fields are compared at Re = 10,000.
infographic.watch_item: The dataset targets Re = 10,000 and provides only one instantaneous 3D DNS snapshot per body, limiting assessment of generalization and time-resolved 3D dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Turbulent wakes behind nine bluff-body shapes from direct numerical simulation and particle image velocimetry
